citations.quote:
Fix integers $n,m\ge1$ and coefficient matrices $A_0,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. The **grade-$m$ matrix polynomial** is
$$P(\lambda):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^j.$$
When $P$ is not identically zero, its actual degree is the degree of its largest nonzero scalar entry and can be smaller than the declared grade $m$; the zero polynomial has no actual degree. It is **regular** when the scalar polynomial $\det P(\lambda)$ is not identically zero. Write $x^*$ for conjugate transpose, $\langle u,v\rangle:=v^*u$ for the Euclidean inner product, $\|x\|_2:=(x^*x)^{1/2}$ for the Euclidean vector norm, and $\|M\|_F:=(\sum_{r,s}|M_{rs}|^2)^{1/2}$ for the Frobenius matrix norm.

The **grade-$m$ homogeneous polynomial** is
$$P_h(\alpha,\beta):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\alpha^j\beta^{m-j}.$$
A projective parameter $[\alpha:\beta]$ is a nonzero pair $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb C^2$ modulo common multiplication by a nonzero scalar. A **homogeneous eigenpair** is $([\alpha:\beta],x)$ with $x\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$ and $P_h(\alpha,\beta)x=0$. This condition is independent of the representative because $P_h(c\alpha,c\beta)=c^mP_h(\alpha,\beta)$. If $\beta\ne0$, the associated finite parameter is $\lambda=\alpha/\beta$ and $P_h(\alpha,\beta)=\beta^mP(\lambda)$. The point $[1:0]$ is the parameter at infinity; there $P_h(1,0)=A_m$, so it is an eigenvalue exactly when $A_m$ is singular. For regular $P$, the algebraic multiplicity at a finite $\lambda_0$ is the order of the zero of $\det P$ at $\lambda_0$. The **reversal** is $P^{\rm rev}_m(\mu):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_{m-j}\mu^j=\mu^mP(1/\mu)$; the algebraic multiplicity at infinity is the order of the zero of $\det P^{\rm rev}_m$ at $\mu=0$. The order of a zero at $0$ is the largest integer $r$ for which $\mu^r$ divides the scalar polynomial.

Let $P(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^j$ be as in [[def-matrix-polynomial-and-homogeneous-eigenpairs]]. For $m\ge1$, define $mn\times mn$ block matrices $A_c,B_c$ by
$$A_c:=\begin{bmatrix}A_{m-1}&A_{m-2}&\cdots&A_0\\-I_n&0&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\ddots&\vdots\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\0&\cdots&-I_n&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad B_c:=\begin{bmatrix}-A_m&0&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\cdots&0\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\0&\cdots&0&-I_n\end{bmatrix}.$$
The **first Frobenius companion pencil** with the sign convention used here is
$$L(\lambda):=A_c-\lambda B_c=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda A_m+A_{m-1}&A_{m-2}&\cdots&A_0\\-I_n&\lambda I_n&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\ddots&\vdots\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\lambda I_n\end{bmatrix}.$$
For a vector $x\in\mathbb C^n$ and finite $\lambda$, its **companion lift** is $z(\lambda,x):=(\lambda^{m-1}x,\lambda^{m-2}x,\ldots,\lambda x,x)^T\in\mathbb C^{mn}$; when $m=1$, this is simply $x$.

derivations.claim: For $m\ge2$, partition the columns of $L$ as $u=(z_1,\ldots,z_{m-1})$ and $x=z_m$, and the rows as the top block row and the lower $m-1$ block rows; write the resulting blocks as $L=\begin{bmatrix}C&E\\D&G\end{bmatrix}$. The lower-left block $D(\lambda)$ is upper block-bidiagonal with $-I_n$ on its diagonal and $\lambda I_n$ on its superdiagonal. Thus $D=-(I-\lambda S)$ for the nilpotent upper block shift $S$, so $D^{-1}=-(I+\lambda S+\cdots+\lambda^{m-2}S^{m-2})$ is polynomial and $\det D=(-1)^{n(m-1)}$. The lower equations with zero right-hand side are $Du+Gx=0$; solving them gives $z_j=\lambda^{m-j}x$. Substitution into the top row shows that the Schur complement is $E-CD^{-1}G=P(\lambda)$. To compute the determinant, swap the top and lower row groups, with sign $(-1)^{n^2(m-1)}$, obtaining $\begin{bmatrix}D&G\\C&E\end{bmatrix}$. Left multiplication by $\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\-CD^{-1}&I\end{bmatrix}$ has determinant one and gives $\begin{bmatrix}D&G\\0&P\end{bmatrix}$, whose determinant is $\det D\det P$. Since $\det D=(-1)^{n(m-1)}$, the total sign is $(-1)^{n^2(m-1)+n(m-1)}=(-1)^{n(n+1)(m-1)}=1$, so $\det L=\det P$. For $m=1$, $L=P$ directly.

For the partition in step 1.1, left multiplication by $\begin{bmatrix}I&-CD^{-1}\\0&I\end{bmatrix}$ clears the top-left block and leaves $P$ in the top-right block, since $E-CD^{-1}G=P$. Left multiplication of the lower rows by $D^{-1}$ makes the lower-left block $I$ and the lower-right block $H:=D^{-1}G$. Right multiplication by $\begin{bmatrix}I&-H\\0&I\end{bmatrix}$ clears that lower-right block; a block-column permutation then gives $\operatorname{diag}(P,I_{(m-1)n})$. Each operation and its inverse has polynomial entries and determinant a nonzero constant, so their products are unimodular.

Put $L_h(\alpha, eta):= eta A_c-\alpha B_c$. If $ eta
e0$, then $L_h= eta L(\alpha/ eta)$, so step 1.1 gives $\det L_h= eta^{mn}\det P(\alpha/ eta)=\det P_h(\alpha, eta)$. Both sides are polynomials in $(\alpha, eta)$. Fix any $ eta
e0$; the identity holds for every $\alpha$, so their coefficients in powers of $\alpha$ agree. Each such coefficient is a polynomial in $ eta$ and agrees for every $ eta
e0$; as univariate polynomials with infinitely many common values they are identical, so the identity holds also at $ eta=0$. For finite $\lambda$, the lower rows of $L(\lambda)z=0$ force $z_j=\lambda^{m-j}z_m$; if $z
e0$ then $z_m
e0$, and the top row is $P(\lambda)z_m=0$. Conversely, for each nonzero $x$ with $P(\lambda)x=0$, the lift in [F2] is nonzero and the lower rows vanish while the top row is $P(\lambda)x$. At infinity, $L_h(1,0)=-B_c=\operatorname{diag}(A_m,I_n,\ldots,I_n)$, so its kernel consists exactly of $(x,0,\ldots,0)^T$ with $A_mx=0$.

For the reversal pencil $\mu A_c-B_c$, reorder the block columns as $(z_2,\ldots,z_m,z_1)$. Its lower equations are $z_i-\mu z_{i-1}=0$; on the first $m-1$ reordered block columns their coefficient matrix is lower block-bidiagonal with $I_n$ on its diagonal and $-\mu I_n$ on its subdiagonal, so its determinant is $1$ and its inverse is polynomial by the finite nilpotent-shift expansion. Solving these equations gives $z_i=\mu^{i-1}z_1$; substitution into the top row gives $\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_{m-j}\mu^j=P^{\rm rev}_m(\mu)$. The same row elimination, normalization by this polynomial inverse, column clearing, and block permutation used in step 2.1 therefore give $\operatorname{diag}(P^{\rm rev}_m,I_{(m-1)n})$ by unimodular polynomial matrices. For $m=1$ the reversal pencil equals $P^{\rm rev}_1$ directly.

The reversal determinant identity is $\det P^{\rm rev}_m(\mu)=\mu^{mn}\det P(1/\mu)$. If $d=\deg\det P$, write $\det P(\lambda)=c_d\lambda^d+\cdots+c_0$ with $c_d\ne0$; then $\det P^{\rm rev}_m(\mu)=c_d\mu^{mn-d}+\cdots+c_0\mu^{mn}$, whose zero order at $0$ is exactly $mn-d$. Step 3.1 shows the reversal pencil has the same zero order, and step 2.2 identifies the homogeneous companion spectrum and eigenspaces. In the permutation expansion of $\det P(\lambda)$, every product has $n$ factors of degree at most $m$; degree $mn$ can occur only by taking the $\lambda^m$ coefficient from each factor, so its coefficient is $\det A_m$. Thus invertibility of $A_m$ is equivalent to $d=mn$ and no infinity eigenvalue; singularity gives $d<mn$ and positive multiplicity at infinity. The geometric multiplicity is $\dim\ker A_m$ by step 2.2 and is not used to infer the zero order.

derivations.claim: From the lower residual equations in [F2], $z_{k-1}=\lambda z_k-e_k$. Back-substitution from $x=z_m$ gives $z_j=\lambda^{m-j}x-\sum_{k=j+1}^{m}\lambda^{k-j-1}e_k$ for $1\le j<m$; when $j=m$ the same formula has an empty sum.

Substitute these expressions into the top row from [F2]. The terms containing $x$ sum to $\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^jx=P(\lambda)x$. For fixed $e_k$, its coefficient is the negative of $\sum_{j=m-k+1}^{m}A_j\lambda^{j-m+k-1}$: the $z_1$ term contributes $-(\lambda A_m+A_{m-1})\lambda^{k-2}e_k$, and each $z_j$ term for $2\le j<k$ contributes $-A_{m-j}\lambda^{k-j-1}e_k$. Thus $e_1=P(\lambda)x-\sum_{k=2}^{m}Q_k(\lambda)e_k$, which is the claimed identity.

We first derive the finite-dimensional Euclidean estimates used here. For $u,v\in\mathbb C^d$ with $v\ne0$, set $c:=\langle u,v\rangle/\|v\|_2^2$. Direct expansion gives $\|u-cv\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2-|\langle u,v\rangle|^2/\|v\|_2^2\ge0$, hence $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$; if $v=0$ the inequality is immediate. Since $\|u+v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|v\|_2^2+2\operatorname{Re}\langle u,v\rangle\le(\|u\|_2+\|v\|_2)^2$, taking nonnegative square roots gives $\|u+v\|_2\le\|u\|_2+\|v\|_2$. For any matrix $M$ and vector $v$, apply the derived inner-product bound to each row of $M$ and $\bar v$ to obtain $|(Mv)_r|^2\le(\sum_s|M_{rs}|^2)\|v\|_2^2$; summing over rows gives $\|Mv\|_2\le\|M\|_F\|v\|_2$. Now put $y=e_1+\sum_{k=2}^mQ_ke_k=P(\lambda)x$. Repeated use of the derived triangle inequality gives $\|y\|_2\le\|e_1\|_2+\sum_{k=2}^m\|Q_ke_k\|_2$. Applying the rowwise matrix estimate to each $Q_k$ gives the claimed bound. For the companion lift, each lower row vanishes by construction and the top row is $P(\lambda)x$.

To see why no uniform unscaled transfer factor follows, take the fixed scalar polynomial $P(\lambda)=\lambda^2+1$. For any $t>0$, set $x=t/(t^2+1)$, $z_2=x$, and $z_1=tx-1$. Direct substitution into its first companion pencil gives $e_1=tz_1+z_2=0$ and $e_2=-z_1+tz_2=1$, while $P(t)x=t$. Hence the block-pencil residual norm is $1$ and the polynomial residual is $t$, which is unbounded as $t\to\infty$. Any error or conditioning comparison must retain the displayed coefficient and parameter scaling.

thm-exact-coefficientwise-weighted-backw.claim: For any nonzero homogeneous projective parameter and nonzero vector, the weighted Frobenius backward-error infimum is attained and equals the residual divided by the vector norm and weighted homogeneous coefficient norm.

citations.quote:
Let $P(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^j$ be regular of grade $m$, let $[\alpha:\beta]$ be a projective parameter, let $x\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$, and choose positive weights $\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_m$. Write $r:=P_h(\alpha,\beta)x$. The **coefficientwise weighted Frobenius backward error** is the infimum
$$\eta_F(P,[\alpha:\beta],x;\omega):=\inf\left\{\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}\frac{\|\Delta A_j\|_F^2}{\omega_j^2}\right)^{1/2}:\ \sum_{j=0}^{m}(A_j+\Delta A_j)\alpha^j\beta^{m-j}x=0,\quad \Delta A_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\right\}.$$
The perturbations of distinct coefficients are unrestricted and measured in the displayed weighted product norm; no symmetry or other coefficient structure is imposed. Replacing $(\alpha,\beta)$ by $(c\alpha,c\beta)$ for $c\ne0$ multiplies the constraint by $c^m$ and leaves its zero set unchanged, so the infimum depends only on $[\alpha:\beta]$. The infimum is defined for finite and infinite projective parameters. The next theorem proves that it is attained and gives its exact value.

citations.quote: Let $\mathbb C(\lambda)$ denote the field of quotients of complex scalar polynomials. Let $R(\lambda)\in\mathbb C(\lambda)^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$ be a square matrix whose entries are rational functions of $\lambda$. Write each entry as a reduced scalar fraction (common polynomial factors have been cancelled), and let $q(\lambda)$ be the monic least common multiple of their denominators. Thus the zero set $\mathcal P:=\{\lambda:q(\lambda)=0\}$ is exactly the set of poles of at least one entry. Define the pole-free domain $\Omega:=\mathbb C\setminus\mathcal P$ and the polynomial matrix $N(\lambda):=q(\lambda)R(\lambda)$, whose entries are polynomials as in [[def-matrix-polynomial-and-homogeneous-eigenpairs]]. A **rational eigenpair** is a pair $(\lambda,x)$ with $\lambda\in\Omega$, $x\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$, and $R(\lambda)x=0$; its $\lambda$ is a rational eigenvalue. The **cleared-denominator polynomial equation** is $N(\lambda)x=0$, but it represents the rational eigenproblem only on $\Omega$. Any solution at a pole is an inadmissible candidate, even when the cleared polynomial matrix is singular there.

derivations.claim: If $\lambda\in\Omega$, then $q(\lambda)\ne0$ by [F1]. Multiplying $R(\lambda)x=0$ by the nonzero scalar $q(\lambda)$ gives $N(\lambda)x=0$. Conversely, if $N(\lambda)x=0$, division by the same nonzero scalar gives $R(\lambda)x=0$. This proves the stated equivalence exactly on $\Omega$.

If $\lambda\in\mathcal P$, then at least one entry of $R$ has a pole by the reduced common-denominator definition in [F1], so $R(\lambda)$ is undefined and $(\lambda,x)$ is outside the rational eigenproblem's domain. A singular value of $N(\lambda)$ cannot change that domain condition; hence every cleared root at such a point must be rejected.

citations.quote:
Fix integers $n,m\ge1$ and coefficient matrices $A_0,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$. The **grade-$m$ matrix polynomial** is
$$P(\lambda):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^j.$$
When $P$ is not identically zero, its actual degree is the degree of its largest nonzero scalar entry and can be smaller than the declared grade $m$; the zero polynomial has no actual degree. It is **regular** when the scalar polynomial $\det P(\lambda)$ is not identically zero. Write $x^*$ for conjugate transpose, $\langle u,v\rangle:=v^*u$ for the Euclidean inner product, $\|x\|_2:=(x^*x)^{1/2}$ for the Euclidean vector norm, and $\|M\|_F:=(\sum_{r,s}|M_{rs}|^2)^{1/2}$ for the Frobenius matrix norm.

The **grade-$m$ homogeneous polynomial** is
$$P_h(\alpha,\beta):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\alpha^j\beta^{m-j}.$$
A projective parameter $[\alpha:\beta]$ is a nonzero pair $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb C^2$ modulo common multiplication by a nonzero scalar. A **homogeneous eigenpair** is $([\alpha:\beta],x)$ with $x\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$ and $P_h(\alpha,\beta)x=0$. This condition is independent of the representative because $P_h(c\alpha,c\beta)=c^mP_h(\alpha,\beta)$. If $\beta\ne0$, the associated finite parameter is $\lambda=\alpha/\beta$ and $P_h(\alpha,\beta)=\beta^mP(\lambda)$. The point $[1:0]$ is the parameter at infinity; there $P_h(1,0)=A_m$, so it is an eigenvalue exactly when $A_m$ is singular. For regular $P$, the algebraic multiplicity at a finite $\lambda_0$ is the order of the zero of $\det P$ at $\lambda_0$. The **reversal** is $P^{\rm rev}_m(\mu):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_{m-j}\mu^j=\mu^mP(1/\mu)$; the algebraic multiplicity at infinity is the order of the zero of $\det P^{\rm rev}_m$ at $\mu=0$. The order of a zero at $0$ is the largest integer $r$ for which $\mu^r$ divides the scalar polynomial.

Let $P(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^j$ be as in [[def-matrix-polynomial-and-homogeneous-eigenpairs]]. For $m\ge1$, define $mn\times mn$ block matrices $A_c,B_c$ by
$$A_c:=\begin{bmatrix}A_{m-1}&A_{m-2}&\cdots&A_0\\-I_n&0&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\ddots&\vdots\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\0&\cdots&-I_n&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad B_c:=\begin{bmatrix}-A_m&0&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\cdots&0\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\0&\cdots&0&-I_n\end{bmatrix}.$$
The **first Frobenius companion pencil** with the sign convention used here is
$$L(\lambda):=A_c-\lambda B_c=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda A_m+A_{m-1}&A_{m-2}&\cdots&A_0\\-I_n&\lambda I_n&\cdots&0\\0&-I_n&\ddots&\vdots\\\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\lambda I_n\end{bmatrix}.$$
For a vector $x\in\mathbb C^n$ and finite $\lambda$, its **companion lift** is $z(\lambda,x):=(\lambda^{m-1}x,\lambda^{m-2}x,\ldots,\lambda x,x)^T\in\mathbb C^{mn}$; when $m=1$, this is simply $x$.

Let $P$ be a regular $n\times n$ grade-$m$ matrix polynomial with $m\ge1$, and let $L(\lambda)=A_c-\lambda B_c$ be the pencil of [[def-first-frobenius-companion-pencil]]. A square matrix polynomial is **unimodular** when its determinant is a nonzero constant. The pencil $L$ is a **strong linearization** of $P$ if there are unimodular polynomial matrices $U,V$ with $ULV=\operatorname{diag}(P,I_{(m-1)n})$ and unimodular polynomial matrices $\widetilde U,\widetilde V$ with $\widetilde U(\mu)(\mu A_c-B_c)\widetilde V(\mu)=\operatorname{diag}(P^{\rm rev}_m,I_{(m-1)n})$. Such matrices exist. In particular, $\det(A_c-\lambda B_c)=\det P(\lambda)$; finite eigenvectors correspond by $x\mapsto z(\lambda,x)$; and the infinite eigenspaces correspond by $x\mapsto(x,0,\ldots,0)^T$ from $\ker A_m$ to $\ker(-B_c)$. The algebraic multiplicity of infinity in both problems is $mn-\deg\det P$. Thus if $A_m$ is invertible there are no infinite eigenvalues; if $A_m$ is singular there is at least one, with geometric multiplicity $\dim\ker A_m$, which need not equal its algebraic multiplicity.

derivations.claim: The discriminant is $(1/2)^2-4(1)(2)=1/4-8=-31/4$. The quadratic formula therefore gives the two roots $\lambda_\pm=-1/4\pm i\sqrt{31}/4$. Neither is infinite because the leading coefficient $A_2=1$ is invertible.
Direct expansion gives $\det L(\lambda)=\lambda(\lambda+1/2)+2=\lambda^2+(1/2)\lambda+2=P(\lambda)$, so these two values are precisely the finite companion-pencil eigenvalues.

For either root, $P(\lambda_\pm)\cdot1=0$, and its companion lift is $z=(\lambda_\pm,1)^T$. Multiplication gives $L(\lambda_\pm)z=((\lambda_\pm+1/2)\lambda_\pm+2,-\lambda_\pm+\lambda_\pm)^T=(P(\lambda_\pm),0)^T=(0,0)^T$.

Thus the theorem's degree-defect formula gives infinite algebraic multiplicity $4-2=2$. Also $P^{\rm rev}_2(\mu)=\operatorname{diag}(\mu^2,1)$, whose determinant has a zero of order two at $\mu=0$.

derivations.claim: A state-space realization is $A=[1]$, $B=[1\ 0]$, $C=[1\ 0]^T$, and $D=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, since $C(\lambda I-A)^{-1}B+D=\operatorname{diag}((\lambda-1)^{-1},1)$. Its reduced common denominator is $q(\lambda)=\lambda-1$, so $N(\lambda)=q(\lambda)R(\lambda)=\operatorname{diag}(1,\lambda-1)$.

For every $\lambda\ne1$, $\det R(\lambda)=1/(\lambda-1)\ne0$, so no nonzero vector lies in its kernel. At $\lambda=1$, $N(1)=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ has kernel $\operatorname{span}\{e_2\}$, but $R(1)$ is undefined because its first entry has a pole. By [F2], the cleared root at $1$ is spurious and must be filtered out.
